title: Making sustainability measurable on the CPG plant floor
body_markdown:
## Understanding resource use starts with overcoming data barriers


Focusing sustainability efforts on improvements with a clear operational payoff means first understanding where resources are used (and lost), from processing through CPG packaging.


To accomplish this, teams need[credible data](https://www.belden.com/blog/CPG-Plant-Data-Your-Secret-Weapon-to-Boost-Customer-Loyalty) that connects consumption to production activity so they can investigate avoidable losses and document results for internal leadership reviews and external reporting requirements.


But specific barriers often appear, **making it difficult to find and use this information** , even though it’s already being collected somewhere in the plant.


Data is in silos, hiding the full picture of resource use


The information needed to make the connection between resource use and what was happening in production at the time often sits in separate systems.


Water consumption may be recorded in a utility system, for example, while cleaning records are stored elsewhere. Without matching those records, it’s difficult to tell which cleaning cycles used more water—and to figure out why.


Bringing that information together also **requires[IT and OT teams](https://www.belden.com/blog/Build-connections-between-IT-and-OT-security-to-boost-plant-operations) to agree on how data can be shared securely** . Questions about access to production systems or transferring data to cloud analytics applications can delay those connections, leaving useful information isolated even when it’s already being collected.


### There’s no consistent way to collect and organize data


Older equipment can make bringing information together even harder. Legacy equipment that was never designed to share data may need to add sensors or gateways before that can happen. Other assets already collect data, but extracting it means finding a way to work around proprietary systems to make it available to other applications.


Once data is available, teams need to make sure it **tells an accurate story** . Otherwise:


- If timestamps don’t match, a consumption spike could be attributed to the wrong run.
- If equipment names vary between systems, records have to be manually matched up before teams can compare performance.
- Missing readings can make consumption appear lower than it actually was, leaving teams unable to verify whether a reported reduction represents a real improvement.


### Plant conditions can interrupt data collection


Harsh plant conditions add yet another challenge. Connections need to withstand the washdown exposure or vibration where they’re installed so that teams have consistent access to information for decision-making.


An intermittent connection can leave gaps in the records needed to investigate a problem. Teams may know that consumption increased, for instance, but **lack the readings needed to pinpoint when it happened or connect it to a specific operating event** .
